snippet: Evelyn, Went through the Phase 2 SOW with our ops team and finance this week. Overall we're comfortable moving forward — the scope matches what we discussed on the call two weeks a
body_text:
Evelyn,

Went through the Phase 2 SOW with our ops team and finance this week. Overall we're comfortable moving forward — the scope matches what we discussed on the call two weeks ago and the $185K number is in line with what we budgeted for the diagnostic phase. A few items I redlined in the attached before this goes to procurement for countersignature:

1. Payment terms — I need NET-30 instead of NET-15. Our AP cycle runs on a monthly batch and NET-15 means we'd be cutting a check outside the normal run, which our controller doesn't love. NET-30 gets us into the regular cycle.

2. Data room access — the draft has data access starting "after kickoff." I'd rather your team (sounds like that's mostly Dr. Bose doing the throughput modeling?) have read access to our MES exports starting the same week as kickoff so we don't lose the first week waiting on IT to provision accounts. Our IT director can set this up in advance if you flag the usernames now.

3. One clarifying question on the interim findings memo — is that a working draft for our internal use only, or will it also go to our board? We had a board update scheduled for week 4 and it would help to know if that memo is presentable as-is or needs a different format.

4. Small thing — Section 6 still references "Phase 1 findings" using the old project code MC-2025-11. Should be MC-2026-04 to match the engagement letter.

5. One more from our CFO — she'd like the final report delivered in a format that can be dropped directly into our board deck without a lot of reformatting, meaning charts as editable PowerPoint objects rather than embedded images, since the last time we tried to pull a chart out of a PDF appendix it took our analyst half a day to recreate it. Not a big lift I'd guess, but wanted to flag it now rather than have it come up as a surprise at delivery.

None of these are dealbreakers on our end. If you can turn a clean version with these changes I can get this to our procurement lead by end of week and we should be able to countersign before the 15th. Also — appreciate you and Gordon walking our ops committee through the approach last month, it made this internal approval a lot smoother than Phase 1 was.

Talk soon,
Bob

Bob Vandergriff
VP Operations, Meridian Castings, Inc.
(815) 555-0142

subject: Re: Halberd Packaging — hours running over budget
snippet: Lucia, Thank you for raising this directly — you're right to ask, and I owe you a full explanation rather than a vague reassurance. I went back through Kyle's and Fiona's time logs
body_text:
Lucia,

Thank you for raising this directly — you're right to ask, and I owe you a full explanation rather than a vague reassurance. I went back through Kyle's and Fiona's time logs this morning with our office manager before writing this, so let me walk you through exactly where the hours went.

The original scope, as you say, was 120 hours built around mapping the three core production processes we discussed in kickoff. Two things happened that weren't in the original plan. First, in week two your plant manager asked us to extend the mapping to the packaging line as well, on the logic that the bottleneck we were finding upstream might actually originate there. That's a reasonable ask and I don't fault him for it, but it's genuinely additional scope — we estimate it added about 26 hours. Second, we had two full-day site walkthroughs that ran long because your second-shift supervisors weren't available during the originally scheduled windows, so Kyle and Fiona had to come back on separate days rather than combining the visits, which cost us roughly another 14 hours in travel and setup overhead we hadn't planned for.

As of yesterday we're at 142 of the 120 budgeted hours, with an estimated 18-24 hours of work remaining to close out the deliverable properly, which puts the likely final total somewhere around 160-166 hours against a 120-hour budget.

Here's what I'd propose. The packaging-line extension was a genuine scope change that your team requested, so I think it's fair for that piece (the ~26 hours) to be billed as a modest change order — call it $9,800 — rather than absorbed by us. The scheduling-related overrun (the ~14 hours plus whatever portion of the remaining work is attributable to it) I think is fair for us to eat, since better planning on our side could have avoided some of it even given the supervisor availability issue. Concretely: I'd like to invoice the original $68,000 fixed fee in full, add a single change order of $9,800 for the packaging line extension, and absorb the rest ourselves rather than billing it. That keeps the fixed-fee spirit of our agreement intact while being honest about the one piece that was a genuine scope addition on your side.

I'm glad to walk through the time logs on a call if that's useful, or just take this by email if it's clear enough as written. Either way, I want you to feel like the fixed fee actually meant something here, not just a number we abandon the moment it gets inconvenient.

Evelyn

Evelyn Thorne
President, Thorne & Cadwell Advisory
(312) 555-0119

meta.action_summary: Evelyn proposed a $9,800 change order for the packaging-line extension while absorbing the scheduling-related overage.

subject: AME Chicago Chapter — Fall Manufacturing Summit speaker invite
snippet: Dear Evelyn, My name is Denise Whitcomb and I coordinate programming for the AME Chicago Chapter's Fall Manufacturing Summit, which this year runs September 15-16 at the Renaissanc
body_text:
Dear Evelyn,

My name is Denise Whitcomb and I coordinate programming for the AME Chicago Chapter's Fall Manufacturing Summit, which this year runs September 15-16 at the Renaissance Schaumburg Convention Center. I'm reaching out because your name came up twice independently — once from a member who attended your session at our spring roundtable, and once from Marta Klein at Ridgefield, who mentioned the process work your firm did there when I asked around for speaker recommendations focused on mid-market manufacturers specifically, which is a gap in our usual programming.

I'd like to invite you to join a panel on Day 1 (September 15th, 2:00-3:15pm) titled "Lean Without the Fortune 500 Budget: Operational Excellence for Mid-Market Manufacturers." The format is a moderated panel with three practitioners — so far confirmed are a plant director from a tier-two auto supplier and an operations VP from a mid-sized food processor — followed by 20 minutes of audience Q&A. We typically get 80-120 attendees in that room, mostly plant managers, ops directors, and a handful of owner-operators from companies in the 50-500 employee range, which I understand overlaps closely with your client base.

Logistics: we cover a modest honorarium ($750) plus one night at the Renaissance if you'd like to stay over rather than commute, and of course a full conference pass so you can attend other sessions and network. We'd need a short bio (100 words or so) and headshot by August 1st for the printed program, and I'd like to get 20 minutes on the phone with you and the other two panelists sometime in early September to align on what ground each of you will cover so we're not duplicating material on stage.

A little more on the audience, since it might affect how you'd want to pitch the material: about a third of the room last year were owner-operators rather than hired ops leadership, so questions tend to skew practical and skeptical of anything that sounds like a big consulting engagement — "what can I actually do Monday morning" is the recurring theme in our post-session surveys. Panelists who lean into concrete, low-cost first steps rather than a full transformation pitch tend to score much better with this crowd than the ones who sound like they're selling a retainer. I mention that only because I think it plays to your strengths given what Marta described, not because I think you need the advice.

I know this is a bit of a leap of faith without having seen you present, but based on what I've heard I think you'd be a strong addition to this particular panel. Would you be willing to join us? Happy to hop on a call if you have questions about format, audience, or anything else before deciding.

Best,
Denise Whitcomb
Programs Committee, AME Chicago Chapter
programs@ame.org

subject: Re: Meridian diagnostic data — throughput analysis
snippet: Evelyn, About 80% through the modeling — attached is the working draft with what I've confirmed so far, and I want to walk through the headline finding because it's more interestin
body_text:
Evelyn,

About 80% through the modeling — attached is the working draft with what I've confirmed so far, and I want to walk through the headline finding because it's more interesting than I expected going in.

I pulled six weeks of MES data across all three of Meridian's production lines and normalized for shift patterns and the two planned maintenance windows in that period. Line A (core casting) is running at 94 seconds average cycle time against a theoretical target of 78 seconds, giving it 71% utilization, with Station 4 — the cooling stage — as the clear local bottleneck. Line B (finishing) is actually in decent shape at 84% utilization, 61 seconds against a 55-second target, constrained mildly at Station 2 (deburr) but nothing dramatic.

The real story is Line C, the satellite line at the Rockford facility. It's running at only 58% utilization, 118 seconds against a 90-second target, and the constraint is Station 1, mold prep, which is running almost entirely manually while the equivalent stations on Lines A and B have partial automation. Because Line C feeds into downstream shared packaging capacity, the model suggests this is actually the binding constraint on total plant throughput, not Line A, which is what everyone on the plant floor assumed going in. Closing even half the gap at Station 1 — without any capital investment, just changeover and staffing adjustments — could add an estimated 12-15% to overall plant output. That's a much more useful finding for Bob's board update than "we found some inefficiencies," and it's the kind of thing that justifies the fixed fee on its own.

Remaining work: I still need to validate the Line C numbers against a second data pull since the sample size there is thinner (fewer shifts logged, Rockford runs two shifts not three), and I want to sanity-check the maintenance-window exclusions with their plant engineer before I call it final. Should have a validated final version to you by Monday.

One more thing worth flagging now rather than burying it in the final report: if the Line C finding holds up under the second data pull, it changes the framing of the whole recommendations section. The original brief assumed we'd be recommending investment across all three lines roughly proportionally. If Line C really is the binding constraint, the honest recommendation is probably to concentrate almost all of the near-term operational changes there and treat Lines A and B as secondary, which is a more concentrated, less balanced-sounding story than what I think Bob's team may be expecting walking in. Wanted you to have that heads-up before Monday so it's not a surprise in the readout, and so you can decide how you want to frame it for the board update.

Anil
